title: Why Rote Learning Is What Kept Me in Teaching
author: Caiti Wade
summary: Caiti Wade answers an Australian newspaper headline claiming a rote learning mandate is driving new teachers out of the profession by describing how explicit instruction kept her in it. As an exhausted first-year teacher building every resource herself, she planned to quit until she joined Ballarat Clarendon College, where lessons were centrally planned and taught from shared slides. She gives five reasons the approach sustained her: students could remember and do what she taught, regular mini-whiteboard checks showed her what every student knew, differentiation became responsive support within one lesson instead of three different tasks, behaviour became easier because students were busy and succeeding, and a predictable structure left room for her personality. She is careful to say that a 90-slide deck alone does not transform teaching and that other teachers' experiences are valid. Her closing point is that debates about teacher retention should ask whether teachers have the conditions, resources and support to thrive, not whether they have too many PowerPoints.
points: Regular retrieval and spaced practice replaced the false assumption that performance in a lesson equals learning, and students retained and built on far more content.
Viewing 30 to 100 mini whiteboards per lesson let her see where every student erred and adjust her explanation in real time rather than discover problems at assessment.

Differentiation moved from assigning different tasks, which risked lowering the ceiling for weaker students, to adjusting guidance within one core lesson, with the rule that if in doubt, provide too much guidance.
Behaviour was easier to manage because students were busy responding every minute or so and felt competent, and the saved effort let her focus on delivery and relationships.
Centrally planned resources cut preparation load and freed her to bring her own humour and flair, which she frames as the opposite of robotic teaching.
quotes: But there’s a difference between watching students successfully complete a task in a lesson and having them actually retain or learn something. Earlier in my career, I wasn’t always particularly good at distinguishing between the two.
If the accusation is that ‘rote learning’ involves students remembering what we’ve taught them, then frankly, I don’t know why that ever became something we were supposed to apologise for doing.

I was viewing somewhere between 30 to 100+ mini whiteboards of student attempts at questions every single lesson. Every time I taught a new skill, I could see almost immediately where students were making errors, what those errors were, and, most importantly, I could immediately adjust my teaching to correct those errors.
I’ve said it before, but there is a real irony in taking the students who need the most support and giving them the least exposure to the content they need.
The instructional harm of too much guidance for a student who doesn’t need it is far less than the instructional harm of not providing enough guidance to a student who does need it.
My students are busy throughout most of the lesson. I sometimes joke that they don’t have time to bend the rules.
Evidence should inform what we do, but it doesn’t have to dictate who we are while doing it.
I didn’t need more freedom to write lessons or come up with a never-before-seen activity to teach linear equations. I needed the time, knowledge and support to become a better teacher.
The approach so often criticised for turning teachers into mindless robots actually made me feel like I could be more myself in the classroom.
